summaries.example: Imagine saying, “I promise to feed the cat.” You are not only making sounds or describing something. You are making a promise. If you say it in the right situation and mean it, your words can create a promise. Austin called this kind of thing a speech act: something people do with words. The promise may also make your friend trust you. That result is another part of what happened.
summaries.summary: John Langshaw Austin was a philosopher who studied language, truth, and the things people do when they speak. He believed that philosophers should examine ordinary words carefully before building large theories. Everyday language contains many useful differences, such as the differences between asking, warning, promising, and stating. Austin also argued that whether a statement is true can depend on the circumstances and purpose of its use, not just on the sentence by itself. His account of speech acts distinguishes three connected activities: producing meaningful words, using them with a particular force, and producing effects in listeners. These ideas helped shape later philosophy of language.
key_ideas: Austin thought philosophers should pay close attention to how people actually use words.
A sentence’s words alone may not settle whether what someone says is true. The situation, purpose, and audience can matter too.
Speaking can involve several actions at once: saying something, doing something with it, and causing an effect.
Austin separated the act of saying something from the force of saying it and from the results it produces.
He also thought that complicated cases cannot always be placed neatly into simple boxes such as true or false.
summaries.why_it_matters: We use words to cooperate, make plans, ask for help, give information, and change relationships. Austin’s work helps us notice that communication is more than putting facts into sentences. It also involves intentions, situations, rules, and effects on other people. This can help us listen more carefully and avoid treating every complicated statement as simply true or false.

important_terms.definition: A thing a person does by speaking, such as asking, warning, promising, or stating something.
A speech act in which a speaker says something with a particular job or force, such as asking a question or making a promise.
An effect that words have on listeners, such as making them believe something or take action.
A judgment about whether what was said fits the facts well enough in a particular situation.
A careful study of the words and expressions people really use in everyday situations.

questions_to_think_about: Can the same sentence do different things in different situations?
When does saying “I promise” really make a promise?
Can something be useful or accurate without being perfectly true?
What might happen if we ignored the way people use words?

summaries.example: Suppose a teacher says, “The project is due Friday.” In one setting, this may be an assertion about a deadline; in another, it may function as a warning or instruction. The sentence’s meaning matters, but the circumstances, purpose, and recognized role of the speaker also matter. Austin’s framework asks us to distinguish the locutionary act—the meaningful utterance itself—from the illocutionary act, such as asserting or warning, and from perlocutionary effects, such as persuading students to begin work. The same words can therefore participate in different acts and receive different kinds of assessment.
summaries.summary: John Langshaw Austin’s philosophy of language examines how ordinary linguistic practices bear on philosophical questions about truth and meaning. He argues that philosophers risk overlooking important distinctions when they move too quickly from particular judgments to general theories. In his account of truth, a sentence is not assessed in isolation: descriptive conventions connect it with types of situations, demonstrative conventions connect an utterance with a particular situation, and human judgment determines whether the match is sufficient for the purposes at hand. This makes room for statements that are accurate, rough, exaggerated, or misleading without fitting neatly into an unqualified true/false contrast. Austin’s study of speech acts develops a related insight. Speaking involves a locutionary act, an illocutionary act with a particular force, and possible perlocutionary effects. His provisional constative/performative distinction breaks down because utterances of both apparent kinds can be assessed in several ways. The entry presents Austin’s position as influential but also open to competing interpretations, especially concerning truth, performative language, and the relationship between meaning and force.
key_ideas: Austin’s method begins with careful attention to ordinary judgments and the distinctions embedded in ordinary language, while leaving room for later theory.
He rejects the idea that sentence meaning, combined with facts in a simple way, always determines a truth-value. Circumstances, purposes, and the way a sentence is used also matter.
His account of truth appeals to descriptive conventions linking sentences with types of situations and demonstrative conventions linking particular utterances with particular situations.

Austin’s early contrast between constative and performative utterances does not remain a simple division. Both kinds of utterance can be defective, and performative-looking utterances can also involve assertions.
The locutionary–illocutionary–perlocutionary distinction separates content, communicative force, and consequences. A single utterance may involve more than one kind of act.
Austin’s treatment of truth can make “true” seem like a broad label for more detailed appraisals, but the entry notes that the exact extent of his deflationism is difficult to settle.
summaries.why_it_matters: Austin’s distinctions remain useful wherever words both communicate and act: classrooms, law, promises, warnings, public announcements, and ordinary conversation. They encourage us to ask what a speaker said, what the speaker was doing in saying it, and what happened as a result. His approach also cautions against forcing complex uses of language into rigid categories. At the same time, the entry shows that Austin’s proposals generate unresolved questions about whether truth is explanatory, how context contributes to meaning, and whether linguistic acts can be cleanly separated.

important_terms.definition: The production of a meaningful utterance, considered through its sounds, grammar, words, and content.
An act performed in saying something, identified by its force, such as asserting, questioning, warning, or promising.
An effect produced by saying something, such as persuading, frightening, informing, or causing someone to act.
A view that treats truth as a thin notion connected with more specific appraisals such as correctness, adequacy, or fairness.
A convention connecting a sentence with a general type of situation, event, or way for things to be.
A convention connecting a particular utterance with a particular situation, event, or thing in the world.
A problem in which an utterance fails to perform the intended act at all, often because the situation or procedure is unsuitable.
A case in which an act is performed but is defective because, for example, it is insincere or improperly used.

questions_to_think_about: Does a sentence have a fixed truth-value apart from the occasions on which people use it?
Can a promise be successful even when it is not sincere? What kind of defect would that be?
Is persuading someone part of the speech act itself, or an effect that follows from it?
Does Austin’s criticism of a simple true/false division eliminate truth, or make truth more context-sensitive?
How might a philosopher’s conclusions change after examining ordinary uses of words more closely?

summaries.example: A student says, “I’ll bring the poster tomorrow.” If the student says this while agreeing to a group plan, the words may count as a promise, not just a prediction. The promise can be unsuccessful if the student is not in a position to make it or is not sincere. It can also have effects: teammates may trust the student and stop worrying. Austin would separate the meaningful words, the act of promising, and the effects on the teammates.
summaries.summary: John Langshaw Austin examined how language works in real human activities. He held that philosophy should begin by noticing the detailed distinctions people make in ordinary speech, rather than assuming that every important question can be answered with broad labels. This matters especially for truth. Austin argued that a sentence does not automatically receive one truth-value simply because it has a meaning and there are facts in the world. The occasion, the speaker’s purpose, the audience, and the way the words connect with a particular situation can affect whether the resulting statement is accurate, rough, exaggerated, or misleading. Austin’s most famous contribution is his analysis of speech acts. When people speak, they may produce meaningful words, perform an act such as asking or promising, and cause an effect such as persuading or frightening someone. His proposed distinction between constative and performative utterances turns out to be difficult to maintain: statements can go wrong, and performative-looking utterances can also contain truth-assessable claims. The broader lesson is that language is an activity, not merely a set of labels for facts.
key_ideas: Austin studied ordinary language because its careful distinctions can help uncover mistakes in philosophical arguments.
What a sentence does depends on more than its dictionary meaning. Context, speaker, audience, purpose, and relevant facts can all matter.
He first contrasted constatives, which seem truth-assessable, with performatives, which seem to do something. He later showed why this contrast is not a simple dividing line.
The three types of speech act describe different parts of communication: content, force, and effects.
Austin’s view of truth allows statements to be rough, exaggerated, accurate, or suitable for one purpose but not another.
His ideas influenced later philosophy of language, even though scholars disagree about how to interpret some of his claims.
summaries.why_it_matters: Austin’s work helps explain why communication can succeed or fail even when the words seem clear. A promise, warning, question, or statement has a social role, and that role depends partly on circumstances. His analysis is useful for thinking about misunderstandings, responsibility, agreements, and public communication. It also teaches a philosophical habit: examine specific cases carefully before deciding that a simple rule explains every use of language.

important_terms.definition: An action carried out through language, including stating, asking, promising, warning, or requesting.
The act of producing an utterance with recognizable words and content.
The communicative action performed in speaking, such as promising, warning, asking, or asserting.
A result caused by an utterance in an audience, such as belief, fear, persuasion, or action.
A statement’s fit with facts, judged in relation to its circumstances, purpose, and use.
A mistake in which an attempted speech act does not happen successfully at all.
A defective speech act that happens but is inappropriate, insincere, or otherwise flawed.

questions_to_think_about: What is the difference between saying that you will do something and promising to do it?
Can the same words be appropriate in one situation and misleading in another?
Why might an utterance fail even when its grammar is correct?
Are the effects of speech under the speaker’s control?
Should every statement be judged only as true or false?
